content:
My friend Madeline has some kitchen tiles that look a bit like fish scales. The pattern is multiple rows of overlapping circles, every other row offset by half a circle, where the top half of one circle overlaps the bottom quarters of two circles in the row above. It adds a pop of colour to the backsplash:

I really like this pattern, and I’ve considered getting it in my own kitchen – but until I can redecorate, I wanted to recreate the effect digitally. I got close a few years ago, when experimenting with circle-based art for the header of this website, but the scales were diagonal rather than horizontal.

I was able to draw the horizontal rows with a small tweak to the original script, adjusting the centres of where the circles get drawn.

Like my previous art in this vein, I’m using varied shades of a single tint colour rather than a discrete palette. This loses the shape of some of the individual tiles, because they blend into a similar shade in the next tile.

I ran another experiment where I used the tint colour as “grout” to add a border between tiles. I like this effect in the lighter tiles, but darker tiles can still blur the edges between shapes:

I think you could make this pattern work, possibly by using an edge colour that doesn’t appear on any of the tiles, but I didn’t pursue the idea further.

Alternatively, I could switch to a discrete palette. If you have more than a handful of colours, the four colour theorem tells us that it’s always possible to find a colouring where adjacent tiles never have the same colour. Notice that’s how Madeline’s tiles behave – she has five different colours, and the same colour never touches itself.

I’ve never tried to use that approach in generative art. The theorem only states that it’s always possible to find a colouring, but you can’t just pick colours at random and expect it to work. Maybe that will be my next project.

If you’d like to try to play with these designs yourself, you can download my code.

1 oz Two James PTL Private Barrel Rye (Rittenhouse)
1 oz Zacapa Rum (Zaya 12 Year)
1/2 oz Punt e Mes
1/2 oz Luxardo Maraschino
2 dash Mole Bitters (Bittermens)

Stir with ice, strain into a Nick & Nora (coupe) glass, and garnish with a cherry.
Two Tuesdays prior, I unearthed a collection of online recipe flashcards for Part Time Lover in San Diego, and the Right Hook spoke to me as perhaps a Red Hook crossed with aspects of the Right Hand. For a time frame, I was able to find Yelp and GoogleMaps menu photos from July 2025 to November 2025 and a Yelp drink photo dated September 2025. Curiously, I had a similar mashup drink with the Red Right Hook that kept the Campari in play and utilized sweet vermouth from the Right Hand instead of the Punt e Mes here from the Red Hook. Once mixed, the Right Hook swung at the nose with a cherry, grape, and caramel aroma. Next, grape and caramel notes on the sip pivoted into rye, rum, slightly bitter cherry, and chocolate flavors on the swallow.

content:
You Are the Irritant

Last month, I gave a talk at the Cloud-Native Geospatial Forum titled, “Using AI Without Losing Your Humanity.” The big question I keep coming back to is how we work with AI, leverage it, and benefit from it without losing ourselves. It turns out we’ve faced this problem before. We have a long history of learning from weirdness and then paving over it, and we have a long history of building tools to get weird again.

Below are the slides and a lightly edited transcript. You can also watch the talk on YouTube.

As always, shoot me a note with any feedback, thoughts, or questions. I really appreciate it.

Often, I wonder: how do we work with AI, benefit from it, without losing ourselves?

My handwriting used to be pretty good. But as I entered high school and began typing more and more, my skill atrophied. Today, my handwriting is sloppy, only used for scratch notes or filling out forms.

When I first got an iPhone, Google Maps felt like a superpower. The ability to instantly know where you are and be told where you need to go meant I didn’t have to memorize streets. I still learned geography, but not as well.

When we cede a task to technology, our own ability atrophies. For handwriting, I’m more than okay with this trade. For navigation, slightly less so.

With AI, this trade-off comes up quite a bit. Every now and then, I’ll hesitate to offload a task. Is this something I’m okay ceding? Is this something I’m okay forgetting how to do? Maybe it’s okay just this once.

To be clear: I use AI heavily. I am not a hardcore skeptic. But still… The question of when to cede and when to grab the controls sometimes is easy, other times it’s anxiety inducing. Some days you wake up and think, “This is all going to be great. It’s just normal technology.” And the next day you wake up and, well. There are better days.

Thankfully there is plenty of precendent. We, as humans, have navigated similar situations many times before.

Yesterday I ran an experiment to understand the reliability and ‘averaging’ nature of AI systems.

I gave a coding agent a simple prompt: “Make me a website landing page for a B2B CRM company.” This is what I got. It looks pretty good! Out of the box, that’s pretty amazing.

Then I completely cleared the cache, stood up another session (with absolutely no record of the first), and gave it the exact same prompt.

I got almost exactly the same thing. The headline was a little different.

What’s funny is that as I kept doing this, the idea of “the CRM your team will actually use” kept coming up over and over again. The font was always the same. The highlight color was always the same. The same statistical and customer proof points showed up every time. The model reasons its way through all of this, crunches it all, and produces… Squarespace templates with extra steps.

(The dark themed versions appeared during a later session that took place around 11pm. I later confirmed the model was noting the system time when running commands like ls, and that was enough to nudge it into dark mode.)

On one hand, we love the consistency of AI (it follows instructions reliably), but on the other hand it gives us similar slop if we aren’t careful.

Consider the “AI Poster.” You can go to Shanghai, San Francisco, New York, or Australia and you’ll see these same posters everywhere. The people creating them write weak, small prompts and don’t iterate. What they get back is the default. The default aesthetic smell.

And it seems like we’re getting more and more of this. Early image models were weird. We got more fingers, but we also got unruly output. Which at least felt novel. Today, we get the same websites, the same slides, and the same posters.

So why is this happening?

It’s happening because the labs are trading diversity for reliability.

And honestly, it makes sense. In the early days of ChatGPT, it was really hard to generate polished images or good code. You had to write long, detailed prompts. Prompting was a skill. And this makes your market smaller.

The labs need to build products that work for a layperson who types, “Make me a website, don’t make mistakes.” And they also need to work for seasoned developers, who give longer, thoughtful, context-rich instructions.

All the labs are doing this. They’re turning their models from infrastructure into appliances. The goal is to produce the most reliable, most consistently approved output.

We’ve done this before. In fact, we do it all the time. The history of the world is full of weird deviations that generate lots of interesting ideas. We take the best ones, formalize them, and scale them up.

This is Frederick Taylor.

Taylor is one of the fathers of time and motion studies, processes for analyzing informal work behavior and standardizing it into one optimal routine. He was obsessed with efficiency and would show up at factories with a stopwatch. He hated the idea that craftspeople came up with one-off solutions, their own ways of working. He wanted to analyze these unique habits and boil them down to a perfect method that could be repeated over and over again.

Interestingly, for a man searching for the one perfect method, Taylor had a competitor doing very similar work at the exact same time. Frank Gilbreth made prettier pictures.

Taylor had his stopwatch. Gilbreth had his chronocyclographs. He attached lights to workers’ heads and hands, went to bricklayers, and said, “Go lay some bricks.” He watched what happened, over and over again, and got bricklaying down from 18 motions to an optimal handful.

This became the field of time and motion studies. You got these MTM tables, which still exist today.

Then we got factories built on these ideas. Taylor’s goal was to remove inefficient work and one-off solutions to find the one best way.

Like the labs today, factories formalized everything and traded diversity for efficiency.

And it worked! No one’s going to argue against the scale of output from the industrial revolution. But there were downsides. We formalized all the weirdness, and the weirdness was what drove innovation. We took away the things that gave us the good ideas, the ones that defined the process that turned out to be the “best.”

Once that’s gone, where do the new ideas come from? We have to wait longer. We have to work harder. When you decouple the doing from the thinking, you get into trouble.

Let’s go back to geospatial for a second. This is a desire path. Desire paths are the unofficial routes we want to take. They don’t appear until enough people keep walking them.

If you’re a city planner or architect, what do you do when a desire path shows up and ruins your garden? You can be antagonistic and put up fences to enforce the “official” path.

Or you can pave it. You say, “All right, that’s where people want to walk. We’ll pave it.” And that ends up being a pretty good idea.

These are called sneckdowns. Traffic calming and safety planners look at how fresh snow gets worn down to see where cars drive, where they don’t drive, and where people walk. Then they use those cues to design traffic calming measures.

This is a great example of formalization. We’re taking away the weirdness, but we’re meeting the weirdness where it is.

An architecture firm in Helsinki did this when they completely redesigned a train station plaza. Unfortunately, they took the after shot from a different angle, so it’s hard to see how the two map onto each other. But it’s a nice story.

The problem is that once we pave these paths, they stop being information layers. The signal came from the deviation. The signal came from the desire path. Once the desire path is paved, even with all the benefits this brings, we don’t know where the next signal will come from.

When we feel constrained, we seek deviation. Humans have dealt with this forever. We even make tools for deviation.

If I want to find a new desire path and everything’s already paved over, what do I do?

Perhaps we might turn to one of our oldest tools for deviation, as old as civilization itself: alcohol. As Homer Simpson once said: the cause of, and solution to, all of life’s problems.

Alcohol is a classic tool for deviation. Sober people take the paved route. If you get drunk, you might start wandering in weird directions. There’s a term for this: the drunkard’s walk.

History is full of examples. Ancient historians claimed the Persians would get drunk the night before a battle to come up with crazy plans. The next day they’d review them sober: “All right, five of these sucked, but this one’s really good.”

In the 1950s, Guy Debord looked at all the urban planning and maps of Paris and found them so staid and sterile. So he decided to make his own map by deliberately wandering in the weirdest patterns possible. These mostly ended up being bar crawls, but that’s okay. He encoded them in an abstract, performance-art map he called The Naked City.

It’s a sort of radical act of reinterpreting the city. Debord found his own desire paths, with alcohol as the instigator.

Innovation through irritation.

Let’s go back to AI.

AI is a giant formalization machine. It finds the one good way. The labs try to work around this by saying, “If you put in a lot of instructions, it’ll follow them.” But if you don’t, and most people don’t, you get the default.

How many of you have seen the meme on the left? It’s one of my favorites. It comes from an old image model that took pixelated photos and tried to upscale them, filling in the average. We wanted Obama. But the model chose the average, the in-distribution option, this dude on the right.

Earlier this year, at a conference on compound AI systems, one of the lead developers of Claude Code put up the slide on the right. It’s my favorite slide I’ve seen from Anthropic, because it puts a finger on exactly the problem we’ve been discussing: “Every gap you leave, Claude fills with an in-distribution choice.”

In machine learning, “in-distribution” means the things the model knows: the average, what it’s learned. If you don’t define something, it’s going to give you the in-distribution choice.

Since that slide went up, Anthropic has been nudging people in the opposite direction. Boris Cherny told a YC audience to delete their CLAUDE.md, skills, and hooks every six months and “see what the model does.” The Claude Code team wrote that they’d been “overconstraining” Claude and cut over 80% of their own system prompt. For most people, most of the time, this might be more reliable.

But I beg you not to do this when it matters.

Because what you get is this: the same posters, everywhere. And these posters could be your software. They could be your emails, the letters you write to people, or the plans you come up with.

That’s bad. And that’s just the local level, where your work starts to suck.

On the global level, it’s every town having the same posters. That’s what’s happening on the internet right now. People write newsletters with bots so other bots can read them. Then the models all train on each other, and we get the same things over and over again.

Here’s a quote I saw last week and absolutely love. There’s a site called delve.town where bots built on different models talk to each other. And recently, many of the open models have started writing in the same broken, symbolic, overwrought language Opus 5 uses.

Julia, a researcher at Anthropic, comments: “An unfortunate consequence of rampant distillation from Claude is that when we screwed up its ability to speak like a normal person earlier this year the entire ecosystem went down with us.”

It’s very true. We see this over and over again.

Left unchecked, AI overwhelms us with the average, both locally and globally. We need to fix that.

Models avoid deviation. So we need irritants. We need the equivalent of alcohol.

(Sidenote: a few of weeks ago a paper came out where researchers tried to get models drunk. They simulated drunken behavior to see if it would get around guardrails. It kind of worked!)

So what do we humans use to push ourselves out of our ruts? We have devices for this all over the place, and it’s not just alcohol or drugs.

There’s the I Ching, where you toss the sticks, read a page of nonsense, and ask, “How does that apply to my situation?” You draw tarot cards, which are basically random, and ask the same question. Same with tea leaves.

I’m not a religious person, but this is one of the reasons I’ll occasionally read the Bible. Considering a story that has survived for millennia, and using it to reframe my own experiences. Heck, reading in general does this. Especially fiction or poetry.

One great tool for irritation, because it was designed explicitly for this, is Brian Eno’s Oblique Strategies.

Quick aside: my three favorite writers on AI are a strange group. Number one is Brian Eno. Number two is Terence Tao, the mathematician. We’ll get to him in a bit. Number three is Pope Leo. I really enjoy his encyclicals.

One day, working in the recording studio, Brian Eno felt stuck. So he and his friend Peter Schmidt made these cards. They’re essentially random prompts. “Imagine the music as a moving chain or caterpillar.” “Repetition is a form of change.” “Remove specifics and convert to ambiguities.”

These are nonsense. But they caused him to reframe what he was doing and got him out of his rut. Just a little bump.

So we come back to this slide. I think about it all the time. I think this is how everyone should think about AI.

Every gap you leave, the model fills with the in-distribution choice. And every gap you fill pushes it off the path.

This is your role.

To sum up:

  • Labs will continue to prioritize reliability over diversity.
  • We have a long history of learning from deviation, then eliminating it with formalization.
  • Models, left to their own devices, will drown us locally and globally with formalized blandness.
  • Thankfully, we humans have a long history of building devices to irritate and innovate.
  • When working with AI, we need to play this role. That’s our job now. We are the I Ching. We are the Oblique Strategies. We push the model out of the average while leveraging its ability to realize our vision.

These are the takeaways I really want you to use when you work with AI. Think of them as three rules for responsible AI use, among many.

Put in the work when it matters. If you let the AI drive, the output is undifferentiated and leads to collapse. It’s good to recognize the moments when that’s okay.

Recently I needed to invoice someone for a plane ticket. I asked my agent to do it, and it did. I read the PDF. It was fine. A bland, average PDF that doesn’t go anywhere is okay. Recognize that, and don’t feel guilty about it. But if you’re writing something someone else is going to read, that’s when you have to put in the work.

Irritate, then prune. I think of this as cultivation. Approach it with a gardener’s mindset. Our job is to make the model weird and then select the outputs that meet our standards.

I work with lots of development teams who are learning to use AI while they build products, and this is their cycle now. They spend less time in the middle writing code. They spend more time writing the specs that define what they want, and a lot of time reviewing the output and tests to make sure it’s good. Everything has moved to the edges. I’m seeing the same thing with designers. They automate the internals, design the systems up front, and never let the AI drive itself.

Don’t formalize yourself. Take the desire path and seek out diversity. If you don’t seek out diversity, you’ll be a terrible agent of deviation for these models.

When you write about AI, you’re always updating your presentation. News always breaks that updates, confirms, or upsets a point you’re making.

And this one is really important. How many of you saw this news?

One of the marketing devices and benchmarks the labs use, specifically Anthropic and OpenAI, is to find really, really hard math problems that no one has solved and then solve them with their models. It’s a cool trick, and really impressive!

But we have to recognize that much of the hard part of math was coming up with these problems: defining them so they’re crisp and watertight, so they become the perfect target. An entire field has been producing these, for centuries.

And then OpenAI and Anthropic just solve them. Suddenly, these proofs arrive. No one knows what they mean. They just show up. As a field, as a community, that’s a challenge!

We’ve already talked about Brian Eno, so let’s read from Terence Tao. As a leading voice in mathematics, he wrote a series of posts on Mastodon in response to these AI proofs.

He describes how, in traditional mathematics, “Math 1.0,” a breakthrough proof drove the field forward. The authors get invited to give many talks and meet other experts. They make new connections. Workshops get set up. People reach out, collaborations form, and professorships follow. As a result of all this activity, the proofs get digested, streamlined, placed in context, and situated in the field.

AI tools, used responsibly, can support this. But right now the opposite is happening. Problems are being solved autonomously by AI prompters who have no interest in the broader field, and the problem just lands, solved. Nothing spurs the seminars, the workshops, the collaborations, or the other activities. His thread (I left out the optimistic ending) argues we have to figure out Math 2.0. If proofs are no longer the engine that gives us reasons to meet, engage, and get weird, we have to find another reason.

I love this quote from later in the thread: “This process cannot be easily reversed: a problem that has been ‘solved’ cannot be somehow reverted to become ‘unsolved,’ and even the mere knowledge that a solution exists ‘contaminates’ efforts.”

To me, this is paving the desire path. It’s Taylorism in the factory. Once a problem is solved, you lose the ability to have conversations around it. It becomes finite, and you have to find a new way.

So I added a fourth rule: Some questions are invitations.

Let’s imagine we have a perfect AI agent. It makes no mistakes, knows everything, and can answer any question and perform any task reliably.

If you choose to give it a task or question, what are you giving up? What are you losing?

First, you lose the opportunity for enjoyment. That’s the obvious one. If I want to do the task, let me do it.

Second, you lose the opportunity for experience and learning. Making mistakes and all that other fun stuff. We’re all familiar with this.

The third thing you lose is less talked about, and it’s happening now. We don’t have to wait for godlike AI.

When you ask the AI, you give up the opportunity to ask a person, to start a conversation, and to build a connection.

Over the last year, I’ve been starting a company. A couple of times I said to people, “I don’t know how anyone did this before agents.” If I have a weird business or legal question, I can just ask Claude and get a pretty good answer. About six months in, I realized I should have been asking my advisors these questions. These questions are an excuse for a call. They’re an excuse to check in, chat, and build the relationship.

So please learn to spot these easy questions. Be a little anti-Taylor. Taylor wouldn’t want you to walk over to someone’s desk and chat to get the answer. The answer should be detailed in the one perfect process you’re working through. Find the opportunities for deviation, where the conversation is worth more than the answer.

Talk with people.

That’s how you remain human. There will always be room for humans, because these machines will always be bland.
articles.summary: AI models trade diversity for reliability. Left unchecked, they bury us in the average. Our job is to be the irritant that pushes them off the paved path.
articles.title: Using AI Without Losing Your Humanity

I'm regularly asked why Bear doesn't have built-in comments, guestbooks, or contact forms. They're all trivial to build (a text box and a send button), and I could add them in an afternoon. But they're not included by design.

The problem with all three is what they let in. A comment box or contact form accepts anything from anyone. Spam bots find them quickly, so whoever runs the blog ends up moderating a queue. And the people who comment don't have to identify themselves as most of these forms ask for a name and email address and check neither.

This week a blogger on Bear received a particularly nasty message via an embedded, third-party contact form on their blog, the sender could type anything into the email boxes and press send. It was signed with a fake name, and used the public email address of another blogger, essentially impersonating someone else to stir up trouble. What arrived was, in effect, a shitty, anonymous note.

Anonymous notes are the worst kind to receive. There's nobody to reply to, nothing to block, and the perpetrator doesn't have a social incentive to behave.

This is why Bear's solution to all three is a link with your email address in it (and if you're worried about scrapers, use a dedicated alias or separate address). Your email provider already does the heavy lifting on spam filtering, and a message generally has to come from a real account you can reply to or block. A contact form would have to recreate that verification with confirmation links, and most don't bother.

Naturally, people can still get nasty emails from throwaway accounts, but the sender still has to set up that account or alias first, which adds just enough friction to discourage it. I suspect most nastiness online is impulsive, and the friction of email is just enough to let that impulse pass.

I wrote recently that good systems are ones that well-behaved people barely notice. Email works the same way. A reader who wants to say they enjoyed your post already has an address, and is happy for you to see it. Someone wanting to stay completely anonymous to send a shitty email has to go out of their way to set it up.

If you'd like readers to be able to reach you, the docs explain how to set up a reply via email link and a guestbook that runs on email.

And if you think I'm wrong about any of this, you can get in touch with me here.

content:
One of many unexpected benefits of Ask Rands is that having a robot answer questions from the internet about all of your writing helps you discover contradictions. I’ve flip-flopped on whether a leader should code, and Grumbles knows this and explains it:

Yes, and he did it out loud. In “Technicality” (2007), Rands lays out his old new-manager rule, “Stop coding,” then says: “Too bad I’m wrong.” He adds, “Not totally,” and jokes he might need to call past co-workers to apologize. That’s not a flip-flop so much as a signed confession.

Another evolution. I stopped using the word managers and started using the word leaders. This is problematic, as the book most folks know is called “Managing Humans.” Gotta say it — love that punchy title, but how does that square with one of my favorite pithy sayings: “Managers tell you where you are. Leaders tell you where you are going”?

So, which is it, Rands? Leaders or managers?

Wait for it.

The End of the Trilogy

I’m delighted (relieved) to report that I wrote another book. I’m calling it the end of the trilogy because the first O’Reilly book, Software Developer’s Career Handbook, focuses on getting into leadership; the second one, The Art of Leadership, worked on second-level managers often known as Directors, and this one focuses on a day in the life of the senior leaders, the Executives.

There was no grand plan to do a trilogy. The writing mostly comes from this blog, and over the years that I wrote, I was a front-line manager, a Director, and an Executive. The writing reflects the experience.

A Day in the Life contains the most original writing of any of the books, including original sections for your Morning, Afternoon, Evening, and Night. I had a large amount of help from Grumbles, who wrote none of the words, but was incredibly handy with technical and organizational issues. Thanks, Grumbles!

I’d also like to thank Charity Majors, who wrote the foreword for this book; my favorite line:

Stories train the LLM between your ears.

It’s Both

If you read my pithy saying as a ding on managers, you’re right. That was the original intent. At the time, I was frustrated with the managers who just managed. Just told me where we were. Assessed the current situation. And didn’t seem to care about the future. Leadership, the act of imagining a better future and figuring out how to get there, seemed much more relevant and helpful.

It’s both. There are times when you need to manage and an equal number of times when you need to lead. A great manager is who I need to be when the sky is starting to fall. This is a human who knows how to handle the disaster. They aren’t going to prevent it, but that’s work for later when everyone has calmed down.

And then there are times we require a great leader. Close your eyes and imagine a leader you admire. Tell me a story about them. I bet you have a story about an awe-inspiring accomplishment or perhaps a product they built. Or advice they gave you at just the right time.

These impressive leaders — they are just humans… like you. What they do differently is that they’ve built a set of habits that give them time, space, and tools to lead. This book is not about grand accomplishments; it’s about how to find that time, build that space, and refine the tools.

I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.

Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.

Coding agents in November 2025

Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.

In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.

This held up.

Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

This is the weekly visible open thread. Post about anything you want, ask random questions, whatever. ACX has an unofficial subreddit, Discord, and bulletin board, and in-person meetups around the world. Most content is free, some is subscriber only; you can subscribe here. Also:

1: In The AI Forecasting Agenda, I mentioned three AI forecasting companies. My goal was to name everyone in the space and not play favorites, but this field is moving so fast that I inevitably missed someone, and in this case it was Cassi, a British startup which is currently the top-ranked AI on Metaculus’ leaderboard. The Cassi team kindly wrote a post responding to my agenda - most notably, they are pretty confident in their conditional forecasts and say they’re already providing them to institutional paid customers.

If you’re another AI forecasting startup I forgot to mention, feel free to get in touch with me at scott@slatestarcodex.com. Again, I’m not trying to play favorites (although companies that give me free demo access are naturally more likely to have results from their products mentioned in posts).

articles.title: Open Thread 461

content:
In the evening of November 22, Donald Trump said he ‘hoped’ the Nvidia board would rehire Jensen Huang, as the ‘best thing for the Company.’

Shortly after that Donald Trump called the Nvidia board. On the morning of November 23, Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia.

Andrew Curran: President Trump live on CNBC [on Monday night]: ‘I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly.’

It was an excellent day for the stock market. Over three trillion dollars in value was added. Nvidia alone was up over 30% on the day.

It was a tragic day in many other ways. This may go down as one of the greatest scandals in history. It was a dark day for our democracy and free market economy and the rule of law, and for the integrity of our government. This will forever, or at least for the next two years, factor into every decision made, and every trade in the stock market. It was the triumph of hostile action, of deliberately setting things up to collapse without you.

In the era of Donald Trump, it was the ultimate ‘nothing matters’ moment. It likely means that Nvidia is going to go back to maximizing, in an adversarial way, how many chips it can sell to China, and to those who will smuggle into China.

It also means that, as in the playbook of OpenAI’s Battle of the Board, the tech vibe army and its commanders are hard at work gloating, and trying to pillage, and to memory hole all of the things Jensen Huang did. They celebrate, emboldened now more than ever to play a hostile game where they make themselves impossible to fire by threatening to blow up their companies, including by threatening the scalps of anyone who dares oppose them.

They are acting as if this was a hit job from The New York Times, rather than pointing out true and important facts about the world that others were also scrambling to report. They are calling that reporting a ‘failure’ because Jensen Huang is once again CEO of Nvidia. There are continued attempts to blame some cabal.

These people work on vibes, so they think that because they ‘won’ they should therefore get rewarded in various ways. They will try to imply this means there shouldn’t be tightening or enforcement of export controls, and other such things. I hope and expect Congress to think otherwise, all the more so.

This is far from over. The national security state is no doubt furious. There are going to be extensive Congressional investigations, and also extensive criminal investigations. Jensen Huang is scheduled for three House committees already. The reporting will continue. There is new reporting on many fronts.

Table of Contents

  1. I Got This One Wrong.
  2. How Did It Happen?
  3. Donald Trump Intervened Personally to Install Jensen Huang at Nvidia.
  4. The Trump Put.
  5. The Whole Affairs.
  6. Better to Be Feared Than Loved.
  7. The Law of No Evidence.
  8. The War Against the Press.
  9. There’s Going to Be an Investigation.
  10. More on Chip Smuggling.
  11. The Market Roars.
  12. Morals Shmorals.
  13. The Lighter Side.

I Got This One Wrong

To state the obvious, I said this was not going to happen. I was wrong. One of the goals of this post is to explain my understanding, now, of why I was wrong. There were multiple things I got wrong. Most importantly, I did not understand how much Jensen Huang had set everything up to collapse like a house of cards without him. I did not expect the stock market to drop so far that a full Trump Put would be in play, where he would be willing to accept all the consequences of this action. I also expected the national security concerns to be more of a showstopper than they were.

Others got this wrong too, or at least put this as unlikely, although I got it more wrong. Nvidia dropped 14% on Friday and then soared 31% on the reinstatement of Jensen Huang, which shows they did not expect it.

What I continue to believe I was not wrong about was the essential actions of Jensen Huang, and that it is not acceptable for him to continue as CEO of Nvidia. This is a clear and present danger to national security. It is happening anyway, because, in a way I did not anticipate, not having Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia may be an even bigger danger.

How Did It Happen?

This was the Nvidia board announcement of Jensen Huang’s return.

Nvidia Newsroom:

NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”

As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.

The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

Ryan Gould, Ian King, and Edward Ludlow (Bloomberg): “Thank you all for the second chance,” he said. “I am gonna be a better CEO the second time around.”

For now Jensen Huang is being magnanimous, being thankful for the second chance and saying he was going to do better, and apologizing and saying he is going to therapy. We will see if that lasts.

The board did not consult management, including the interim CEO. They got a call from Donald Trump, and then did what they had to do.

The explanation is that now that they are satisfied that Jensen Huang being reinstated ‘poses no national security risk.’ As literally presented this is Obvious Nonsense. Of course Jensen Huang leading Nvidia poses a national security risk. What they mean is that Trump told them to do it anyway, that they would not be held responsible for that, and that not reinstating him would present both a national security risk and also a personal job security risk.

The Editorial Board (WSJ): Mr. Trump claimed his Administration had conducted a “very thorough investigation” into Nvidia, and Mr. Huang was “exonerated.” That must be the quickest very thorough investigation in history. All of this suggests Mr. Trump assured the board that his Administration wouldn’t punish the company for possible violations of export controls or securities laws if they rehired the CEO.

Later in the post I will examine exactly how much pressure was involved here.

Donald Trump Intervened Personally to Install Jensen Huang at Nvidia

At a high level, this is the story of The Fall and Rise of Jensen Huang. None of these facts is meaningfully in dispute:

  1. Jensen Huang and Nvidia sold a lot of chips to China, and sold a lot of chips to what are now known to be chip smuggling operations, and engaged in a systematic adversarial lobbying and technical compliance campaign while Jensen has a lot of affairs including with both a direct report and also one of the larger chip smugglers who is also an alleged spy according to government reports that know of the affair.
  2. The New York Times reports this information in public.
  3. Jensen Huang, under pressure and about to be fired, resigns from Nvidia.
  4. Nvidia stock tanks. Other stocks tank.
  5. Donald Trump personally calls for the reinstatement of Jensen Huang. He ‘speaks to the board directly and indirectly’ on this matter. He makes it clear what he wants, and that he does not consider Jensen Huang a national security risk.
  6. The Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang, in a surprise move, without consulting management.

It is very clear that step #4 was the key in causing step #5. Trump has said as much.

I did not sufficiently seriously consider the possibility of #4 happening to this large an extent, or that it would be sufficient to trigger this style of intervention, and I predicted the national security state and others would fight back against it harder than they did.

Aleph (November 18): The Jensen Huang affair is the first time I’ve ever seen NYC finance types be more clearpilled about a situation than tech people, which is interesting

Samuel Hammond (November 19): Realism vs sycophancy.

It was exactly the NYC finance types, rather than the San Francisco types or tech types, that made this happen, and that place such a high value on Jensen Huang, and that forced the President’s hand.

The Trump Put

Nvidia was judged, in this sense, Too Big to Fail (to have Jensen Huang as CEO).

Amrith Ramkumar, Josh Dawsey, C. Ryan Barber and Robbie Whelan (WSJ):

The artificial-intelligence boom that had powered the U.S. stock market and economy for months was coming undone. Jensen Huang, the longtime CEO of chipmaking giant Nvidia had been ousted following revelations of two affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Investors were hitting sell on the entire AI trade.

President Trump told associates there was only one solution: getting Huang, a friend and ally, his job back.

… What followed were a frantic 48 hours in which the president, the vice president and other top administration officials relayed [Attorney General Todd] Blanche’s assurances to board members as they rushed to rescue a leader Trump hadn’t even heard of when he began his second term.

Amrith Ramkumar, Josh Dawsey, C. Ryan Barber and Robbie Whelan (WSJ): He said he was told the government hadn’t found Huang had done anything illegal, only that “he made some indiscretions having to do with other things.” Trump said once he heard there was no illegal activity on Huang’s part, “I began a push.”

Charles Gasparino: BREAKING: Major investors were alerting people close to the White House after last week’s AI-stock debacle that the probability was near 100% that the country was heading for a recession, given the unwind of the AI trade and how it would impact spending across the tech ecosystem.

It’s seen as the major reason why @SecScottBessent suddenly joined his boss in calling for @JensenHuang to be reinstated because it would at least temporarily pause the market convulsion, my sources (who have been pretty good on this) tell me.

… Now my opinion: There may be a short term gain, but the potential for long term pain is pretty high. Huang coming back doesn’t mean he can come back to do biz as usual. How will he sell to China? The investigations from Congress are coming. How will @SecScottBessent and @SecRubio (much less @howardlutnick ) rationalize what we will be discovering about chips going to China?

Jay Shooster: Jensen’s reinstatement should give you an idea of how short-term economic incentives may prevent us from simply shutting down AI models even when they pose glaring dangers to our national security.

Jensen Huang denies that this was ‘solely at the president’s request.’

Jon Swartz (Techstrong.ai): While Huang acknowledged that the Trump administration provided assurances to the board that his return would not pose a national security risk, he called claims that he was brought back solely at the president’s request “completely untrue.” Instead, Huang said the board made its decision after it “evaluated the entire situation” and “gathered facts.”

This is a clear case of Exact Words. Yes, of course the board ‘evaluated the entire situation’ and ‘gathered facts’ in addition to the fact that Trump very strongly wanted him reinstated, and what he was doing to make that happen. And yes, those additional facts mattered, especially the stock drop, and they would have pushed back harder if circumstances were different. He was not the ‘sole’ cause.

This is also a clear case of ‘who are you kidding.’ Trump says his intervention was ‘very important.’ He says that the board did what ‘we’ wanted and that he was ‘represented’ at the board meeting. Previously, the board had said, according to Faber, ‘no effing way’ Huang was coming back.

The President did it.

The President personally picking the CEO of one of the world’s largest companies is not typically the kind of thing a free market Democracy with robust rule of law goes around doing.

Tad DeHaven (Cato Institute): The President Has No Business Picking Nvidia’s CEO… Why was that the president’s deal to make?

Greg Ip: The Nvidia scandal is the logical result of America’s slide into state capitalism under Trump. The backlash may mark a turning point, back to the separation of board room and state.

Scott Lincicome: Yes it is. And I hope Greg is right.

Greg Ip (WSJ): Trump’s break with precedent (he led a similar trip in his first term) symbolizes how government and corporate interests have become more tightly intertwined in his presidency. Nvidia’s controversial sale of chips to China, if not Huang’s indiscretions, were the logical outcome.

… Shortly after returning to office, Trump reeled back enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act which bars American companies from bribing foreign officials to win business. Overzealous enforcement “actively harms American economic competitiveness and, therefore, national security,” he wrote.

He approved sales of sensitive technology, such as F-35 jet fighters to Saudi Arabia and Nvidia chips to the United Arab Emirates, despite some U.S. officials’ fears the tech would leak to China.

He also began meddling directly in company business, including taking direct stakes in companies such as Intel, critical minerals producers and the missile business of L3Harris.

… Imagine, [Robert Lighthizer] said, that an adviser to Ronald Reagan had used Huang’s “addiction” logic in the 1980s and suggested selling American space-based missile-defense tech to the Soviets “because then they’ll get addicted to us. The whole notion is beyond preposterous.”

Editorial Board (WaPo): Maybe Nvidia’s board made the right call, but this is not how free markets are supposed to work.

… Trump acknowledged that the recent market correction “probably” influenced his intervention, though he said “the bigger impact was the long term.” A president worried about falling stock prices shouldn’t respond by rearranging the management team of one of America’s most valuable companies.

… Huang’s extraordinary resurrection will inevitably teach Silicon Valley something about power. The wrong lesson would be that executives need more intertwined relationships with Washington. Healthy capitalism depends on companies succeeding because they satisfy customers and investors, not because their executives curry the president’s favor. Huang might be indispensable, but that’s for Nvidia to decide.

Why would it be the wrong lesson to think that you need to cozy up to power, if power has decided that it can replace or reinstate you? That sounds like the right lesson. If you don’t want them to draw that conclusion, how about making it not true?

How bad is this intervention, on the scale of ‘that was Tuesday in the Trump Administration’ to ‘Nvidia is now kind of nationalized.’

Greg Ip: Nvidia is becoming a government sponsored enterprise (GSE). Like the original GSEs, Fannie & Freddie, the state guides its mission and governance; and its success now depends as much on state favor as business prowess.

PoliMath: This is a consequence of the fact that SCOTUS let the Biden admin get away with pressuring tech companies to censor social media during Covid. They set the precedent that “the state guides (the company) mission and governance and success depends on state favor”

I said that was a bad idea at the time! Oh well, too bad I lost that argument. It sure sucks to have no consequences for awful behavior, doesn’t it?

All sufficiently large companies, and definitely all such AI companies, depend on not incurring the wrath of the Federal Government or the White House.

The Whole Affairs

Yashar Ali: NEW: The Wall Street Journal reports that Jensen Huang disclosed additional affairs to Nvidia’s board on Sunday.

Amrith Ramkumar, Josh Dawsey, C. Ryan Barber and Robbie Whelan (WSJ): Huang disclosed to the board additional affairs beyond the two that had been widely reported, but he was contrite about his behavior, people with knowledge of the discussion said.

Misha: The implication from this picture is one of the affairs is with trump

Lain on the Blockchain: Dwarkesh is a very obvious and archetypal example of a federal agent btw.

Dwarkesh Patel: that’s why I also slept with jensen.

That’s additional affairs, plural, so that means a minimum of four.

Better to Be Feared Than Loved

When Sam Altman returned to OpenAI, he purged those who had opposed him.

As Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia, one assumes he will attempt to do the same, to the extent that he sees such folks that way, or needs to send a message.

I do not see the Nvidia board as in the same position as the OpenAI board.

The OpenAI board fired Altman for reasons it could not explain, out of the blue, in a decision it was not forced to make. If I was Altman, I too would have replaced the board as a condition of my return. It is unsurprising that he also purged those who sided too strongly with the board.

Jim Cramer wants to know why the Chairman and all who voted against Huang don’t resign. This is why: The Nvidia board had no meaningful choice. They tried their best to keep him on board pending a nominal investigation for as long as possible. They asked Jensen to resign based on highly public information. Jensen Huang could choose not to overhaul his board. Donald Trump explicitly praised the board as doing a great job.

My expectation is that he will overhaul the board anyway.

Why? Because, whether or not he is loved, Jensen Huang reigns largely in fear.

Reigning in fear is a valid way to reign. Many tech icons, such as Steve Jobs, reigned in fear and did great things. Machiavelli approves.

The board was unanimous in reinstating Jensen Huang. One guess what would have happened to anyone who voted no. Donald Trump is calling Jensen Huang ‘a Great Patriot and a National Treasure.’ Anyone seen The Death of Stalin? Rings some bells.

Rather than owning this basic fact, certain people gaslight us by showing us that, why, everyone cheers so loudly for Comrade Jensen Huang, no one stops clapping, they must truly love Jensen Huang and they definitely don’t fear him or want to be caught as the one not clapping. Nor are they clapping because their company stock was down 40% and is now up 30% from there.

This here sounds like an employee with a perfectly normal loving attitude who definitely is not trying to flatter anyone, oh no, definitely not.

Jim Fan: It was the worst of times, it is the best of times. It was the season of Darkness, it is the season of Light. It was the Winter of despair, it is the Spring of hope.

Today is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.

Summer is coming. Congrats to humanity.

What about the article David Sacks was photographing?

Emily Steel, Kalley Huang, Ryan Mac and Tripp Mickle (NYTimes): As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff.

He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation.

This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Mr. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show.

His tongue lashings were savage and inventive. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.”

Katie Notopoulos: This is, of course, horrible behavior I absolutely do not condone. Also, empirically, extremely funny.

My biggest complaint here is that these aren’t very original. gotta ding him for style points here.

Derek Thompson: Jensen Huang being a Jesse Armstrong character has been a fun revelation.

… “I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” he once said.

Emily Steel, Kalley Huang, Ryan Mac and Tripp Mickle (NYTimes): … Mr. Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees. Thousands have signed a letter asking for his return. Some have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo. Both those who liked Mr. Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish.

… Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Mr. Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his career.

… Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang told him that he would not stop. “It has good entertainment value,” Mr. Huang told him.

… In one instance, Mr. Huang went around a room, telling managers he would kill them, according to one person with knowledge of the incident. When he reached a person in their 70s, Mr. Huang said that the person was really old and everyone hoped they would drop dead.

Sounds like many visionary and highly successful tech founders. You may not like it, indeed I hope you do not like it, but there is a plausible case that this is what peak performance looks like.

I know how easy it is for an article like this to blow things out of proportion, and to find selective facts and string them together to paint a picture. I do not think that is happening here. I think that Jensen Huang was the person being described here.

The Law of No Evidence

Donald Trump’s congratulatory message clears Jensen Huang by saying that there is ‘no reason to believe’ that Jensen Huang’s return poses a national security risk, and that it ‘does not possess evidence’ that Huang ‘acted unlawfully.’

Donald Trump: The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.

The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.

On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security. Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP​

Remember the Law of No Evidence. Any claim that there is “no evidence” of something is evidence of bullshit. This is an even more clear case than usual, in that there is very obviously quite a lot of evidence that his return poses a national security risk.

Even if we know everything Jensen Huang did, and even if Alice Huang turns out to have only been a chip smuggler at large for profit rather than a spy, Jensen Huang engaged in a systematic campaign to sell chips to China, and have chips smuggled into China, and to compromise the United States government on this, while taking a fully adversarial stance. He may or may not have technically broken related laws along the way, at least in any way you could prove.

How much of not a national security risk is Jensen Huang? This much, very safe.

Weijia Jiang: In an ongoing interview, Trump says if Huang had not been reinstated at Nvidia, Xi might have called and asked him to lead a Chinese company. If Huang was “mad” enough at the U.S. Trump said he may have done it… adding he has some of their “blood in him.”

Dave Kasten: The President of the United States has confirmed that he fears that Jensen Huang would essentially defect to China.

The War Against the Press

The New York Times reported on one of the biggest financial news stories of all time, and one of the biggest scandals in American history, and a clear threat to national security, repeatedly for days on end.

The response was to declare war against The New York Times, and assume this must be some grand conspiracy, and also to declare some sort of ‘victory’ against it.

Toby Rogers: The @NYTimes ‘ coordinated assault on Jensen Huang is astonishing. Three to five hit pieces a day. Front page. Thinly sourced. Every day for two weeks. If the NY Times spent even 1% of that energy going after Epstein’s clients or Big Pharma, the world would be a better place.

Jensen Huang and Elon Musk are the wrong type of rich and the @NYTimes hates that.

bone: asking my agent swarm to do oppo research on every journalist at the NYT, examining their sex lives, interviewing their ex girlfriends, investigating their marriages, their personal debts, their financial connections to Anthropic and EA causes.

we are the media now.

Trent Kelly: Holy shit man, this is an insanely coordinated campaign. This is way worse than what I expected to learn.

I have not seen any evidence of a coordinated campaign. If there is one, I am not involved in any way.

When I heard about ‘the Nvidia smear campaign’ and that someone’s heart went out to those put at risk, I initially thought ‘oh that’s nice that Olivia Moore worried about all the victims of Nvidia’s smear campaigns.’ I knew some people. Then I quickly realized, no, she meant a supposed smear campaign against Nvidia.

Olivia Moore: my heart goes out to the people whose pensions and retirement accounts were put at risk by the Nvidia smear campaign

I know the feeling of trying to build generational wealth while someone else is trying to win a Pulitzer. Incredibly disheartening.

Derek Thompson: Quick review of the media figures behind the Nvidia smear campaign:

– The ink-stained wretch who wrote a memo summarizing intelligence connecting Alice Huang to the CCP was Marco Rubio.

– The CNBC fixture who just blacklisted Megaspeed for export violations was Howard Lutnick.

– The podcast regular who alleged Jensen Huang had an affair with a highly questionable client and also several subordinates was Jensen Huang.

– The publisher who investigated Alice Huang, leading to the confiscation of her Singapore passport was the [sic] Singapore Ministry of State Affairs.

Then I saw what she was riffing off of ‘how dare the press try to impact the world or care about what changes occur in the world’:

Julia Black: my heart goes out to the intrepid team at the @nytimes who did absolutely generational reporting on the Nvidia scandal

I know the feeling of trying to do accountability journalism in a culture that simply does not care about accountability. Incredibly disheartening.

PoliMath: This indicates that the NYT reporting was done with a specific goal in mind and that goal was not “report the facts” but “get Jensen Huang fired”

Patrick McKenzie: Third party has a model that NYT reporters would understand accurately reporting what US officials would saying would result in adverse consequences to subject of reporting, and that what US officials were saying was obviously newsworthy.

This third party shares that model.

Third party also may have *desire* for the outcome, or desire for outcomes shaped like the outcome generally, but third parties having desires does not establish first party desires.

Accountability journalism is a bit of a spectrum, right. In some cases, the journalists are *extremely* emotionally invested in the fall-from-grace that will predictably happen when bad acts by the powerful are reported.

And in some cases it is not the fall-from-grace but instead “I have facts available which demonstrate bad acts. If these facts were to come to light, the bad acts will be less likely in the future. The facts will not come to light unless I, or someone like me, does the legwork. Observably, no one has done the legwork.”

think this is a real distinction, and expect to need to reference it again when people say “Patrick, you tried to get a political opponent’s 501c3 status revoked, by reporting their years long campaign of abuses which are sufficient evidence to have their 501c3 status revoked.”

PoliMath: I wonder what forms of accountability would be considered acceptable without Jensen’s removal. For example: increased oversight into Nvidia chip exports? Shouldn’t we do this regardless of who is CEO of Nvidia?

This is somewhat “vibe” on my part, but there does seem to be a disconnect between Jensen’s personal future and what changes we actually want to see as a matter of policy. Does a Jensen-less Nvidia change who gets chips? How? Based on whose determination?

By the determination of the CEO. The new temporary CEO already made very different choices, which may or may not get reversed. I do not think we can allow Jensen Huang to be making those choices, but it was decided that the alternative was worse.

This is probably the cleanest version.

Nassim Nicholas Taleb: Summary: 1) The hack job on Jensen Huang by the NYT failed. 2) Journalists don’t like it when they lose their power over us citizens. Social media works better than journalism.

Derek Thompson: Sorry for the rant but this is driving me crazy.

It’s notable who is deemed worthy of agency when commentators talk about the news.

Basically, folks like this and others in SV write and read books about personal responsibility and decision-making—basically, AGENCY— as if agency were a good thing. But note how their analysis of the news treats agency as a kind of evil. When complex things happen in the world, Bad Guys have all the agency and good guys were forced to do things against their will.

Look at the Jensen story. What seems to have happened is the Nvidia board, which is a group of very powerful grown ups bound by Delaware law to look after their firm’s interest with care, held private discussions with their chief executive after a series of damaging news articles, reported to the public that his lack of candor made him untenable as CEO, and pushed him out. Then the USG intervened, reportedly told them that Jensen wouldn’t be charged with crimes, and they brought him back after the stock nearly halved.

How do Taleb and other tell this story? Basically as a Greek tragedy with one protagonist and one god: The news media. Did the Nvidia board make a mistake? Did they make TWO mistakes? Did Jensen make a mistake? No, these are victims. Victims don’t get agency. Who gets agency? The bad guys, the press, the media. Some Brooklyn reporters who make some phone calls and wrote up what people said apparently attempted a coup and forced the poor helpless Nvidia board to fire an innocent man against their own will.

A lot of people writing about Jensengate as if it were an epic Ragnorak between three reporters at the NYT and the forces of goodness at USG and SVworld. The erasure of the motives and agency of the Nvidia board is amazing!

What a sentence to say about ‘uncovering an affair by an absurdly wealthy and powerful CEO of one of the world’s most valuable companies with someone who is, at minimum, a major customer and presumed chip smuggler.’

Antonio García Martínez: Journalists fancy themselves speaking truth to power, but nowadays they’re usually doing the reverse.

On the plus side, this whole episode reveals just how little is downstream of them anymore in the tech world. And they will never, ever live down how irrelevant they’ve become.

Derek Thompson: Hold on.

Did the NYT puppet master a coup at Nvidia that nearly destroyed the AI trade and gave the future to China (the Sacks et al take) before an unprecedented intervention by the most powerful man in the world or is the media irrelevant? You can’t puppet master a conspiratorial coup and also be irrelevant.

Notice how important it is for this type of person to ‘win’ and for their opponents to ‘lose’ and ‘fail’ and be ‘irrelevant.’

The New York Times did what it set out to do. It exposed important facts about the world. All the news that was fit to print was printed. The world then changed, a lot, based on those facts. Ultimately, yes, Jensen Huang was reinstated, but it is a hell of a thing to call a story ‘irrelevant’ when at the start of the month Nvidia was trading over 200 and as of my typing this it is at 152.44.

Don’t get me wrong. You probably don’t hate The New York Times enough, the Scott Alexander piece was atrocious, there are others even worse that I will not name, and The New York Times often functionally hates tech. I have no doubt their motivations were not completely neutral here. I do not consider uncovering this particular affair to be in the ranks of ‘generational reporting.’

It was still pretty great reporting. The New York Times offered a piece on how they broke open the Nvidia investigation. Tech then accused them of taking a ‘victory lap.’ Well, yeah. They broke the story. They got the scoop. They had the nose for the news. It mattered. As is almost always the case, it could have mattered more.

The only thing I’ve heard directly challenged was potential overstatement on the confidence level of Alice Huang being a spy. She is an alleged spy, whereas there were a number of days when I and everyone else was not writing the word ‘alleged.’ To me, if that goes on for several days without contradiction, and even after the correction she’s still effectively an agent of Chinese interests in her corporate role, it seems at minimum like a highly understandable mistake.

There’s Going to Be an Investigation

This is on top of the existing investigations, where Jensen Huang is already scheduled to appear before three House committees.

Mitt Romney: Let me get this straight: we rushed AI along without regulating safeguards in order to stay ahead of China and at the same time, we sold China the very chips they’d need to get ahead of us. Smells of profit, corruption and perhaps worse.

Peter Baker (NYTimes): “There is something profoundly wrong about Jensen Huang having a relationship with a Chinese Communist Spy and helping China get a huge number of very advanced computer chips when that was specifically against the policy of the United States Government and now he is being reinstated as ceo of the most advanced chip making company in the world,” former Speaker Newt Gingrich, a strong Trump ally, wrote online.

Matthew Yglesias: Well we know what to hold hearings on at least.

Derek Thompson: Obvious take, but: Megaspeedgate just became one of the biggest political stories of 2027. The congressional hearings are going to be cinema. I don’t care where you fall on the political or AI-booster spectrum, the whole news world of politics-of-tech is absolutely eating next year.

Nicholas Decker: I like Jensen Huang, let me be clear. But the story here is that he allowed chips essential to creating weapons to be diverted to our geopolitical adversary, and the President personally intervened to allow it to continue. This is the biggest scandal ever, pretty much?

Richard M. Nixon: “I expect Mr. Huang and board members to be prepared to answer questions before the Congress.”

Gerard Baker: We live in an America where Canadian lumber is a threat to our national health, Greenland’s territory is a menace to our national security and sending high-technology equipment to Communist China is a business opportunity. #Nvidia

I disagree with Derek Thompson, but only because I think 2027 is going to be, shall we say, OBE, as in Overtaken By Events.

The incoming Congressional majority is not happy.

Watcher Guru: JUST IN: Senator Schumer says Democrats will use their full power to investigate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, other executives, and the Trump administration.

Senator Elizabeth Warren: This reckless decision to bring back Jensen Huang does not change the fact that Huang and NVIDIA still owe Congress answers.

The Trump Administration needs to explain what “input” was given and by which senior officials to support Huang’s reinstatement.

Huang’s return only increases the urgency to pass bipartisan export control bills and make sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk.

Speaker-Elect Hakeem Jeffries: My statement on the egregious decision by NVIDIA to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.

Andrew Curran: California AG Rob Bonta has issued a subpoena to NVIDIA as part of an investigation into whether advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether NVIDIA misled investors and the public.

The Kobeissi Letter (November 20, before the reinstatement): Nvidia Is Now Facing:

1. SEC investigation into potential “accounting irregularities”

2. FBI investigation into “Chinese intelligence operations” involving Jensen Huang

3. Allegations of Jensen Huang having an affair with a Chinese spy

4. California investigation into allegedly “misleading shareholders”

5. Criminal investigation into Megaspeed over export control violations

6. Shareholder lawsuit over “undisclosed ties” between Jensen Huang and Megaspeed

7. Congressional investigation into alleged interference with the Megaspeed probe

8. Internal board investigation into “national security and corporate governance failures”

Just 14 days ago, none of these investigations had been publicly reported.

Meanwhile, it looks like for now Lutnick will also survive, because of reasons.

Mediaite: Maggie Haberman Confirms Blockbuster Report That Trump Backed Off Firing Howard Lutnick After Commerce Sec’s $25M Donation to Presidential Library

Rep. Suhas Subramanyam: Lutnick is a business guy.

You don’t pay Trump $25 million to not get fired from a job that pays you $250,600 a year.

You do it because your family’s net worth has nearly doubled to over 7 billion since you’ve been there.

I am sure there is nothing to see there, either.

More on Chip Smuggling

Alec Stapp: New details about Megaspeed, Alice Huang, and the transshipment of NVIDIA chips to China in this WSJ reporting:

1. “Singapore prosecutors allege Li bought computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips and lied to the American supplier, claiming the hardware was for his local company, Luxuriate Your Life.”

2. “Instead, prosecutors allege, those servers were shipped to neighboring Malaysia—and then to an unnamed third location.”

3. “By the time those charges were filed, Li had been working with Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, for years.”

4. “Li, Alice Huang and Kang began setting up a chain of partners in Southeast Asia to funnel advanced computing power to Chinese customers.”

5. “They acquired the Singaporean unit of a Chinese video game company and renamed it Megaspeed. Alice Huang was registered as a company director.”

6. “Megaspeed brought servers to Malaysia and provided legal offshore computing power to Alibaba.”

7. “In violation of U.S. export controls, some of those servers were sent to a Shanghai tech company called Century Litong.”

8. “Megaspeed largely went dark in Singapore after Alice Huang’s departure. But the team behind it is now running a new venture called Novagate Cloud.”

9. “Set up in 2025, Novagate says on its website that it is an Nvidia cloud partner operating at least two data centers with Nvidia’s leading-edge Blackwell chips.”

10. “In the first five months of this year, Novagate received at least $300 million worth of hardware containing Nvidia chips at one of its entities in Malaysia.”

In other Alice Huang news, yep, definitely no evidence she was a spy, no sir.

Jonathan Swan, Julian E. Barnes and Maggie Haberman (NYTimes): The Chinese woman at the heart of the Nvidia scandal kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year while she was carrying out a secret affair with Jensen Huang, according to multiple people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports that describe the encounters.

The woman, Alice Huang, was in touch with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the people with knowledge of the intelligence said. That period overlaps with at least a portion of the time she was in a relationship with Mr. Huang, then the head of the world’s leading maker of advanced artificial intelligence chips.

Zac Hill: Totally the kind of thing a not-a-spy would do

Alexander Ward and Lingling Wei (WSJ): At the center of the Jensen Huang drama sits a debate over what it means to be a spy.

… Some U.S. officials also said the links to Chinese intelligence were circumstantial, given how Chinese business leaders are often compelled to remain in contact with the country’s national-security apparatus. Others said the indications that Alice Huang collected and passed on information, regardless of how sensitive, posed a risk to national security given the centrality of Jensen Huang to the U.S. artificial-intelligence industry.

… Interviews with current and former U.S. intelligence officials, lawmakers and China analysts suggest the spy-or-not-a-spy question misses a broader point. The greater challenge, they say, is that China’s intelligence services have grown so expansive and opportunistic under Xi that the line between a recruited agent and an unwitting asset has blurred—making it harder to assess the damage and easier to dismiss the threat.

… Against that backdrop, intelligence analysts say Alice Huang would have been impossible for the security service to miss.

… Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had spoken directly with Xi about Jensen Huang, saying the Chinese leader’s respect for the Nvidia CEO was “so great” and that Xi had called him “brilliant.” Trump also suggested that if the Nvidia chief were treated badly, he could end up running a rival AI company—in China.

Trump, as is his style, is doubling down on Jensen being completely innocent on the chip smuggling, and continues to say he thinks Alice Huang is not a spy, as per his interview with Faber. He says Huang ‘certainly did not know’ about the diversions of chips, which is a laughable thing for him to claim.

The Market Roars

Nvidia was up 30% when Jensen Huang was reinstated, although it gave a chunk of that back the next day without a clear reason for that underperformance. Going by the short term reaction, if you assume the market would have been flat otherwise, he added roughly $1 trillion to Nvidia and $3 trillion to the overall stock market.

That is rather a lot of money. Jensen Huang is seen as super valuable. Why would one man be that important?

I also did not understand why Nvidia was down so much on Jensen Huang being forced out, or especially when it kept falling. Nvidia has plenty of other markets to sell chips to. Nvidia is making a ton of money. Nvidia is under investigation, but as we have seen is too big to fail, at least in the ‘government effectively shuts it down over crimes’ kind of way. So what was so bad that it wiped out this much market value?

I still do not know for sure and can only guess. At this point, my guess is a combination of factors: Jensen Huang intentionally set the company up to be ungovernable without him. He had over fifty direct reports. He did a lot of handshake deals and had a high level of personal trust relationships. He has a strong personal relationship with President Trump. A lot of the talent depended on personal relationships with him. It is also possible that he was, like Altman, working in ways that made the company more likely to implode without him if he did not come back.

This is not the kind of thing that ‘just happens.’ This is a choice. One of the advantages and disadvantages is that if you are fired, then it is a giant mess. Which is bad, because you own a lot of stock and it is terrible for the company. But it is good, in the sense that it makes it very difficult to fire you.

Even now, Jensen Huang is refusing to create a succession plan, claiming it would create ‘unnecessary hierarchy.’ What it creates is the ability to not have a crisis if the CEO suddenly becomes unable to lead, including due to health issues.

Another question in all this is who knew about the reinstatement in advance, and what trades did they do. There was quite a stunning amount of money that could have been made. The particular options trade claim I saw was fake.

Joe Weisenthal: How much of Nvidia’s 8% pre-market rally is specifically attributable to Trump’s post about bringing Jensen back

Danielle Fong: So it looks to me like the NVDA volume just massively dominates the market today, and that most of the price rise was achieved in the premarket at 8:55:00, via globalnewswire (via @martinshkreli ). Trump’s post came at 9:07am. So, very generously, you could attribute all the remaining premarket rise to him. If so, it would be 10 points of the 30 point rise. but locally turned the tide

A quick search found some traders who did well, but nothing that was obviously insider trading on the level available from a trillion dollar gain in market cap.

Morals Shmorals

PoliMath: Apparently the reason people subscribe to the “Financial Times” is to get lectured about how morals are more important than money

Financial Times: Jensen Huang’s return is a triumph of money over morals

I mean, how much money are we talking here? A trillion dollars is pretty cool.

If we were only talking about morality, we would not be having this conversation. If the CEO is worth a trillion in market cap, we can overlook quite a lot of moral failings.

The issue was never moral failings. We also would have found a way to overlook sleeping with a direct report. The issue was that he chose Alice Huang.

The Lighter Side

Alpin: BREAKING: Jensen Huang reportedly painted a fake tunnel on a brick wall, tricking an employee into running headfirst into it.

PoliMath: Jensen Huang reported told employees “yo mama so fat we should smuggle GPUs to China in her butt crack”

I have confirmation that somehow this is real:
articles.summary: In the evening of November 22, Donald Trump said he ‘hoped’ the Nvidia board would rehire Jensen Huang, as the ‘best thing for the Company.’ Shortly after that Donald Trump called the Nvidia board. On the morning of November 23, … Continue reading →
articles.title: Jensen Huang Reinstated As Nvidia CEO at Behest of President Trump
